reading.title: When a Town Preserves Its Harvest
reading.basis: 当季阅读回忆中出现的食品保存主题
paragraphs: A community kitchen in the fictional town of Bellmere was built to reduce the amount of fruit thrown away after the autumn harvest. Local farms often sold their best fruit immediately, while smaller or oddly shaped pieces remained unsold. Volunteers first collected this surplus and turned it into jam. The work began as a weekend activity, but demand from nearby schools soon made a permanent kitchen necessary.

The organisers did not claim that every preserved jar was cheaper than fresh fruit. Glass containers, electricity and staff training all had costs. Their main goal was to make seasonal food available for longer and to help farmers earn something from crops that might otherwise be wasted. A local college measured the project over two years and found that waste fell, although transport emissions increased slightly because collection vans visited several farms.

The kitchen now teaches residents how to preserve food safely at home. Instructors emphasise clean equipment, accurate temperatures and clear labels showing when food was prepared. They also explain that preservation does not improve poor-quality ingredients. The project has therefore shifted from making products alone to sharing practical knowledge.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says some fruit remained unsold.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 names a local college.

questions.prompt: What was the organisers’ main aim?
options: A. To make every jar cheaper than fresh fruit
B. To extend the use of seasonal food and reduce waste
C. To replace all farm shops
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states the main goal.

questions.prompt: Transport emissions fell during the two-year study.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says they increased slightly.

questions.prompt: What should labels show about the food?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 requires labels showing when food was prepared.

reading.title: A Park Designed With Its Neighbours
reading.basis: 当季阅读重建练习中出现的城市公园改造主题
paragraphs: For years, Alder Park was crossed mainly by commuters taking a shortcut to the station. The city council proposed replacing an unused car park with a garden, a small play area and a wider path. At the first public meeting, residents supported more trees but worried that a narrow entrance would make the park difficult for wheelchair users.

Designers revised the plan after observing how people actually moved through the space. They placed benches near the main path, kept one quiet corner away from the play area and widened both entrances. The new planting uses species that need relatively little watering once established. A volunteer group agreed to record which plants survive their first two summers, rather than assuming that every choice would succeed.

The council will judge the project using several measures: visitor counts, maintenance costs and short interviews with nearby residents. It will also compare temperatures on the new path with those on an exposed pavement outside the park. These measurements cannot prove that the park alone changed the whole neighbourhood, but they can reveal whether the redesign makes this particular route more comfortable.

questions.prompt: Why did commuters previously use Alder Park?
options: A. To reach the station more quickly
C. To avoid a river crossing
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 calls it a shortcut to the station.

questions.prompt: What did residents want improved for wheelchair users?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 mentions the narrow entrance.

questions.prompt: All benches were placed beside the play area.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says benches are near the main path, but does not say all are by the play area.

questions.prompt: How many summers will volunteers monitor the plants?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the first two summers.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of the temperature comparison?
options: A. It cannot measure the park path
B. It cannot establish a neighbourhood-wide effect by itself
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 limits what the measurements can prove.

reading.title: Who Gets to Create Art?
reading.sourceTitle: 是否只有天生拥有特殊天赋的人才可以创作艺术
reading.basis: 由本期写作公开话题延伸的独立阅读练习
paragraphs: People often assume that memorable art can only be produced by individuals born with exceptional talent. Certainly, natural ability may help someone notice colour, rhythm or shape more quickly than others. However, this advantage does not guarantee meaningful work. In the fictional town of Bellmere, a community study found that many admired local artists had shown no unusual skill as children. What they shared instead was sustained curiosity: they regularly observed ordinary life, experimented with unfamiliar materials and remained interested even when their early results were disappointing.

Practice is especially important because artistic techniques can be learned. A beginner may initially struggle to control a brush, structure a story or perform a melody, but repeated effort gradually improves these abilities. For example, Mara Venn, an invented ceramic artist, began attending evening classes at the age of forty-two. Her first bowls were uneven, yet five years of deliberate practice enabled her to develop a distinctive style. Her progress suggests that technical weakness is not a permanent barrier, provided that learners receive useful guidance and continue working through frustration.

The environment also influences whether creative potential develops. Schools sometimes treat art as less valuable than science or mathematics, while families may discourage children from pursuing activities that appear financially uncertain. By contrast, supportive communities provide affordable spaces, patient teachers and opportunities to display unfinished work without embarrassment. Such conditions encourage creative confidence, which allows people to take risks and express personal ideas. Talent may remain invisible when individuals lack time, materials or encouragement, so judging ability without considering opportunity can be deeply misleading.

This does not mean that everyone will become a celebrated painter, musician or writer. People differ in their interests, ambitions and rates of improvement, just as they do in sport or language learning. Nevertheless, artistic creation should not be reserved for a supposedly gifted minority. Its value includes enjoyment, communication and self-understanding, not merely public recognition. Society should therefore widen access to arts education and praise persistence alongside achievement. Natural talent can offer a useful beginning, but curiosity, opportunity and disciplined effort are more reliable foundations for a lasting creative life.

questions.prompt: What quality did the admired local artists share?
questions.explanation: The answer appears near the end of the first paragraph, after the Bellmere community study is described.

questions.prompt: What enabled Mara Venn to develop a distinctive style?
questions.explanation: The answer appears in the second paragraph in the sentence describing her improvement over five years.

questions.prompt: What do supportive conditions encourage?
questions.explanation: The answer appears in the third paragraph immediately after the examples of affordable spaces, patient teachers and display opportunities.

questions.prompt: What may remain invisible when people lack resources or encouragement?
questions.explanation: The answer is the first word of the final sentence in the third paragraph.

questions.prompt: What should society widen access to?
questions.explanation: The answer appears in the fourth paragraph in the sentence recommending how society should support artistic creation.

listening.title: Community Art Workshop Announcement
listening.sourceTitle: 是否只有天生拥有特殊天赋的人才可以创作艺术
listening.basis: 由本期写作公开话题延伸的独立听力练习
sentences: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Community Centre’s monthly talk on creativity and art.
Tonight, painter Lena Morris will challenge the common belief that only naturally gifted people can produce meaningful artwork.
Lena began drawing at the age of thirty-two, after a bicycle accident forced her to spend six weeks at home.
Her first pictures were simple pencil sketches of everyday objects, including a coffee cup, an old shoe, and a houseplant.
She says that regular practice, patient observation, and a willingness to make mistakes helped her improve more than talent did.
During tonight’s session, Lena will demonstrate a technique called blind contour drawing, in which artists study an object without looking down at their paper.
After the demonstration, participants will have twenty minutes to create a picture inspired by a personal memory.
All essential materials are provided, although you may bring your own sketchbook if you prefer.
The workshop is suitable for complete beginners, and nobody will be asked to display their work without permission.
Please meet beside the information desk at seven fifteen, where our volunteer Marcus will guide you to Studio Three.

questions.explanation: The location is stated in the first sentence when the speaker welcomes everyone to the Riverside Community Centre.

questions.prompt: How old was Lena when she began drawing?
questions.explanation: The third sentence says that Lena began drawing at the age of thirty-two.

questions.prompt: What kind of sketches did Lena first create?
questions.explanation: The fourth sentence describes her first pictures as simple pencil sketches of everyday objects.

questions.prompt: How long will participants have to create a picture?
questions.explanation: The seventh sentence explains that participants will have twenty minutes for the activity.

questions.prompt: Where should participants meet before the workshop?
questions.explanation: The final sentence asks participants to meet beside the information desk.

writing.sourceTitle: 大公司借助大型体育赛事推广产品,有人认为这整体上对体育产生负面影响
writing.basis: 由本期写作公开话题延伸的独立写作练习
writing.prompt:
Major sporting competitions increasingly depend on sponsorship from multinational companies, which often use these events to advertise their brands and products. Some people argue that this commercial involvement harms sport, while others believe it provides important benefits.
